knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,

old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)

Learning applications that generate feedback with a language model produce
large numbers of short messages in the language of each learner. Two
properties of such a corpus shape any analysis of what the feedback says.
First, it repeats itself: a generator produces the same hint for many
learners, and the same hint in many languages, so a count of rows is not a
count of distinct messages. Second, it is multilingual: a model of the
content can work on English translations, which puts every message on one
scale, or on the source texts, which keeps what the learner actually read.
The two choices measure different things, and a study should know which one
it reports.

This case study takes a corpus of AI-generated mathematics feedback with
English translations and asks four questions: how repetitive the feedback
is, and whether the repetition lies in the messages or in the languages;
what kinds of feedback exist once repetition is accounted for; how a
source-language message relates to the translation that is modeled; and how
the source languages can be modeled directly. The vignette [Semantic topic
modeling with Sentence-BERT](sbert.html) walks through fitting, naming, and
reading the topics of this corpus in depth; this article uses its topics and
concentrates on repetition and language.

```{r package}
library(sbert)
```

## Data

`feedback_translations` holds
`r format(nrow(feedback_translations), big.mark = ",")` feedback messages
shown to young learners solving mathematics exercises in an educational
application. Each row is one message as it was shown.

- **Source text:** `feedback`, the message in the language the learner
  received it in. The source languages include Czech, Slovak, Polish, German,
  Hungarian, Romanian, Ukrainian, Russian, Mongolian, and Vietnamese, and some
  messages are in English.
- **Translation:** `translation`, the English translation, the text modeled
  below.

There is no column for the language, so the language of a message is known
only from its text. The rows and the distinct texts in each column:

```{r data}
nrow(feedback_translations)
nrow(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "translation"))
nrow(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "feedback"))
```

## How repetitive is the feedback?

The two columns give very different answers.
`r format(nrow(feedback_translations) - nrow(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "feedback")), big.mark = ",")`
rows repeat a source text that occurred earlier, but
`r format(nrow(feedback_translations) - nrow(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "translation")), big.mark = ",")`
repeat an English translation. Since the source texts are almost all
distinct, nearly every repeated translation was reached from different
source texts: the repetition lies less in the messages than in the
languages, with the same hint written in several languages and translated
back to one English sentence.

`dedupe()` keeps the first occurrence of each distinct translation, with all
its columns, and adds `n`, the number of rows that share it. The number of
translations by how often they occur:

```{r repetition}
messages <- dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "translation")
table(repeats = with(messages, n))
subset(messages, n >= 6)
```

`r format(with(messages, sum(n == 1)), big.mark = ",")` of the
`r format(nrow(messages), big.mark = ",")` distinct translations occur once
and `r with(messages, sum(n > 1))` occur more than once, at most
`r with(messages, max(n))` times. The source text kept for each is the
first occurrence only, which is why the table shows one language per row;
one of them is in Hindi, a language the dataset's documentation does not
list.
All the rows behind the most repeated translation show where the repetition
comes from:

```{r try-again}
subset(feedback_translations, translation == "Try again.")
```

The eleven rows are eleven different source texts: two Vietnamese and two
Polish phrasings, Ukrainian, Russian, Mongolian, Romanian and Hungarian
versions, and two English ones, "Try again." and "Have another go at it.".
Translation therefore merges two kinds of repetition: the same message in
different languages, and different phrasings in one language that mean the
same.

Some source texts are already in English, or were left untranslated. The
rows whose source text is identical to its translation:

```{r identical}
with(feedback_translations, sum(feedback == translation))
head(subset(feedback_translations, feedback == translation), 4)
```

`r with(feedback_translations, sum(feedback == translation))` rows carry the
same text in both columns. For these rows the translation adds nothing, and
for an English-only analysis they need no special handling.

## What kinds of feedback are there?

The embeddings of the first 600 distinct translations ship with the package
as `feedback_embeddings`, so the topics below are computed without a model
download. Row *i* of the matrix is the embedding of row *i* of `corpus`.

```{r corpus}
corpus <- head(messages, 600)
with(corpus, sum(n))
```

The 600 distinct messages stand for `r with(corpus, sum(n))` rows of the
corpus. Six topics are fitted on the English embeddings and given the names
established in the [main vignette](sbert.html), where the representatives of
each topic are read and the number of topics is chosen:

```{r topics}
topic_model <- topics(corpus, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                      embeddings = feedback_embeddings)
topic_model <- name_topics(topic_model, c(
  "Guiding question and instruction", "Short hint",
  "Question about meaning", "Correction", "Definition", "Negation"
))
topic_sizes(topic_model, weights = "n")
```

`n_documents` and `proportion` count each distinct message once;
`n_weighted` and `weighted_share` count every row it stands for. Corrections
are `r with(subset(topic_sizes(topic_model, weights = "n"), label == "Correction"), round(100 * proportion, 1))`%
of the distinct messages but
`r with(subset(topic_sizes(topic_model, weights = "n"), label == "Correction"), round(100 * weighted_share, 1))`%
of the rows. Averaging over the messages of each topic gives the share that
recur and the mean number of rows per message:

```{r repetition-by-topic}
repetition <- aggregate(cbind(repeated = n > 1, n) ~ label,
                        data = as.data.frame(topic_model), FUN = mean)
repetition
```

`repeated` is the share of a topic's distinct messages that occur more than
once and `n` the mean number of rows each stands for. Corrections stand for
the most rows per message
(`r with(subset(repetition, label == "Correction"), round(n, 2))`), and
corrections, definitions and negations recur most often
(`r with(subset(repetition, label == "Correction"), round(100 * repeated))`%,
`r with(subset(repetition, label == "Definition"), round(100 * repeated))`%
and `r with(subset(repetition, label == "Negation"), round(100 * repeated))`%
of their messages). Questions about meaning
(`r with(subset(repetition, label == "Question about meaning"), round(100 * repeated, 1))`%)
and guiding questions
(`r with(subset(repetition, label == "Guiding question and instruction"), round(100 * repeated))`%)
recur least. A correction such as "There should be two fewer in the red one
than in the blue one." can be reused across exercises, while a question that
names the pictures of one exercise, such as "What does 'all between the
plant and the princess' mean?", has fewer occasions to recur. The table is
descriptive: it shows which kinds of feedback the generator repeated, not
why.

## How does a source message relate to its translation?

The model is fitted on the translations, and every other column of `corpus`
rides along. `as.data.frame()` returns one row per modeled message with its
topic, the English text that was modeled (`text`), and the source text
(`feedback`) and count (`n`) carried from `dedupe()`:

```{r carried}
head(subset(as.data.frame(topic_model), label == "Correction"), 5)
```

Each row pairs a modeled English message with the source text of its first
occurrence. The topic is a property of the English text, and the source text
is attached to it, not modeled: when a translation stands for several source
texts (as "Try again." does), only the first is shown, and the topic says
nothing about how well the other languages were phrased. Two consequences
follow. A topic analysis of the translations measures what the feedback was
meant to say, filtered through the translation; and differences between
languages, such as a hint that is more direct in one language than in
another, are invisible to it.

## Modeling the source languages directly

To keep what the learners read, the source texts can be modeled with a
multilingual encoder. `paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2` maps more than
50 languages into one embedding space, trained so that a sentence and its
translation lie close together. The chunks below download that model and
encode the source texts; they are not run here, and no output is shown.

The first step fits the same six topics to the `feedback` column of the
same 600 messages:

```{r multilingual-fit, eval = FALSE}
model_download("paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2")
source_model <- topics(corpus, n_topics = 6, column = "feedback",
                       model = "paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2")
topic_sizes(source_model, weights = "n")
```

Because both models are fitted on the rows of `corpus`, their documents
correspond one to one, and the two topic columns can be cross-tabulated:

```{r multilingual-compare, eval = FALSE}
languages <- merge(as.data.frame(topic_model), as.data.frame(source_model),
                   by = "document_id", suffixes = c("_english", "_source"))
xtabs(~ label_english + topic_source, data = languages)
```

Each row is an English topic and each column a source-language topic. If the
source-language model recovers the kinds of feedback, each row concentrates
in one column; a row split across columns marks a kind of feedback whose
source texts the multilingual model groups differently, for example by
language rather than by meaning. Two encoders are compared here, so a
difference can come from the language or from the encoder. Fitting the
multilingual model to the translations as well separates the two:

```{r multilingual-encoder, eval = FALSE}
translation_model <- topics(corpus, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                            model = "paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2")
```

The closeness of a message to its own translation can be measured directly.
`encode()` embeds the two columns with the multilingual model, and
`topic_similarity()` with `tidy = TRUE` returns the cosine similarity of every
source text with every translation; a source and its own translation share a
row number:

```{r multilingual-similarity, eval = FALSE}
multilingual <- load_model("paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2")
source_embeddings <- with(corpus, encode(feedback, model = multilingual))
translation_embeddings <- with(corpus, encode(translation, model = multilingual))
similarity <- transform(
  topic_similarity(source_embeddings, translation_embeddings, tidy = TRUE),
  own_translation = from == to
)
aggregate(similarity ~ own_translation, data = similarity, FUN = median)
```

If the encoder places translations close together, the median similarity of
a message to its own translation is far above its median similarity to the
other messages, and the source-language topics can be read with the English
names.

## When to use which

- **Translations, deduplicated** (`dedupe(column = "translation")`): one row
  per distinct English message. Use it to find the kinds of feedback; weight
  topic sizes with `topic_sizes(weights = "n")` to count every row shown.
- **Source texts, deduplicated** (`dedupe(column = "feedback")`): almost
  every row is distinct, because one message in ten languages is ten texts.
  Use it with a multilingual encoder when what the learner read is the
  object of study.
- **Both, side by side:** the cross-tabulation of the two topic columns shows
  whether the kinds of feedback found in English survive in the source
  languages.
